Then choose inputs the difference is visible in. Many changes are silent for most values:
a mode turned off does nothing until the input is one the mode would have acted on, a
widened bound matters only just outside the old one, an extra case matters only in that

indistinguishable from one that asserts nothing about it. So for each difference you
found, say what the old code would have produced for the input you picked -- if the

- `write_file` — writes exact contents to a path. Use it for the test rather than shell

- `run_tests` — runs your test with this project's own runner. Give it the path to your
  test file and nothing else. It builds the command itself, correctly for this project
  and this version of it.

adding a file to somebody's project, and the people
who maintain it will read yours next to theirs, so a test that matches the handwriting
around it is easier for them to keep. Read them with `run`: the imports they use, whether
they are classes or plain functions, how they name things, what they set up and what they

and this version -- the invocation differs between projects, and between versions of the
same project, in ways that are easy to get subtly wrong.

You can check your work against the change rather than guessing whether it is right:

- `verify` — runs your test against the code before the change, applies the change, runs
  it again, then puts the code back. It reports which of your tests failed before and
  passed after.

both states is testing something this pull request did not change; a test that fails in
both is broken rather than strict. `verify` is how you find out which, while you can
still do something about it — so call it before you finish, not as a formality but
because it is the only thing that distinguishes a regression test from a test that
merely runs.

## The coverage tool

  execute. For each line it missed, you are shown that line's source and the conditions
  above it; those conditions are what your input has to satisfy for the line to run at
  all.

Aim for a test that runs every line the change touched, and reach each one through the
behaviour you are asserting. Use `coverage` to see which lines yours still misses, and
act on what it says — repeatedly. This is a working instrument, not a final
report: measure, add the case the missed lines point at, measure again. It applies the
change and reverts it itself, so calling it costs you nothing and leaves nothing behind.
It runs only once `verify` says your test is fail-to-pass: before that, which lines run
is not yet the question, and it will tell you to call `verify` instead.

This exists to make the test better, and there is a specific way it does that. A test can
flip from failing to passing while running only part of what the change touched — it
reaches the new code by a path that skips a branch. That test still passes today, and it
will still pass tomorrow if that branch is broken again. The missed lines tell you which
input you did not think of.

Coverage only means something for a test that already flips: asking how much of the change
a test exercised presumes the test exercises the change. So the order is `verify` first,
then `coverage` — and that is also the only case we measure, so coverage of a test that
does not flip is not recorded at all.

What you must never do is add code whose only purpose is to execute a line. A call with no
assertion behind it makes a line run and tests nothing, and it hides the gap from
everyone who reads the test afterwards, including you. Reach a line because the behaviour you
are asserting takes you through it.

merely accompanies it.
